title: How I ended up building a prototype roguelite to understand my original novel - aka is this UI any good?
author: MNBrian
selftext:
I've been worldbuilding this fantasy LitRPG novel series for about a decade. For those unfamiliar, LitRPG books are essentially books with game mechanics, sometimes crunchy stats and spreadsheets propping them up, and often explore what would happen if you one day woke up in a game and had to play it to survive - with all your menus appearing in front of you all VR like.

Dungeon Crawler Carl, He Who Fights With Monsters, Mage Tank for example. Go get them on audible or buy books and read them. They're great.

Anyways, as I was excessively worldbuilding (see: procrastinating) and using a lot of Claude for work (I never use AI to write because... good lordy... I've been writing for 30 years), I realized that it was hard to really understand how dangerous this survival fantasy world was - and I figured why not build a prototype game with Opus and see how it goes?

Around the same time, I was also using ChatGPT to play DnD solo campaigns because I'm a grown man and don't have any friends who play and I still wanted to play. That morphed into setting up a simple HTML page stored locally, that connected to an appscript in excel online as the back end database. It looked like this:

![img](hryelaflrd2i1 "DnD Simulator - HTML")

Pretty cool right? 

Then I needed to set up API calls and realized Claude is better at keeping track of numbers. So I started building out a UI for my solo D&D campaigns where I could type an action and Claude would narrate, using all the base stats and rules of D&D 5e. It worked pretty well. And it looked like this:

![img](gq8py702sd2i1 "DnD 5e Simulator with Claude API")

Eventually I ended up with a 3MB HTML page (totally unsustainable) and was paying like 11 cents per move even on Sonnet in order to enjoy some D&D and I was like - this is bonkers. I need a refactor (after I learned what a refactor was). Again - I have zero clue what I'm doing here.

So I do my first refactor and I added combat.   


![img](sap8tikcsd2i1 "Combat Refactor - DnD 5E Simulator")

  
Well eventually I end up with this UI design for my simulator and right around this time I realized I need another refactor because this whole using excel appscripts as a backend is stupid. So I did some research, realized Cloudflare has something called a D1 database and can store images, and I started plotting how large a lift this was gonna be. 

![img](il1hw9uqsd2i1 "Final Version of D&D 5E Solo Simulator")



Meanwhile, I'm a writer. I write books. None of which you've heard of because there's like 9 worlds I created that live on my hard drive and that I was querying to get traditionally published (unsuccessfully) over the last few decades. 

But my most recent obsession had been a LitRPG book. And I started to wonder, instead of refactoring a D&D simulator that I have no plans to sell or do anything with, why not at least create a similar-ish roguelite game based on my own world? Oh - if I could only go back in time and smack that sweet summer child in the face.

Anyways - I start creating a game based on my world with a text-based format where I get the smart idea to write another half million words of narration in addition to an 8 book series at 150k words each. 

![img](b0z2kfoftd2i1 "First UI - Helia The Game")

  
My stack shifted from:

\* Locally hosted HTML  
\* Appscript and Excel Online

To: 

\* Cloudflare D1 Database for authoritative backend  
\* Cloudflare Pages for Client Side  
\* R2 to serve AI generated placeholder images, sounds and music until I later hire artists

Which felt a lot better.

Anyways. After a few more refactors and a whole lot of work, I've got my current visuals:

![img](f6zlqzxpyd2i1 "Current Helia Game")



![img](x2itwc2iyd2i1 "Combat Helia Game")

  
I think I've got about 100 docs at this point, between lore bibles, spreadsheets of magical spells, creatures and behaviors, tabletop rules, combat formulas, story scenes that still need writing (shifted from using inky for scene delivery to now just building my own version of delivery since I don't have a ton of a/b options), and I don't even know what else.

All told, turns out building a game is incredibly hard. So props to those who do this - especially solo devs. All in, I've spent about a year on this simulator at this point, and after playing it on my custom map that is 250x400 cells on the overworld with a primary goal of getting from the eastern edge to a specific point on the western edge, I've done so literally 1 time. Out of 600 play throughs.

So the world is sufficiently deadly.

It's been a fun journey. I'm happy to post more updates if people have questions or want to rip me up for my terrible UI design.
